spans.note: Section 3 heading and Unit of Analysis subheading, with blanks

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad (N=123,868), defined as all encounters between a specific player and referee during the season
the outcome was defined as whether the player received at least one red card from that referee across all their encounters
the sample comprised 123,868 dyads (from 146,028 originally), 1,564 unique players and 2,968 unique referees
17,309 dyads (14.0%) involved dark-skinned players (>=0.75) and 106,559 (86.0%) involved light-skinned players
red card prevalence was 1.26% overall (1,562 dyads), 1.42% among dark-skinned players and 1.23% among light-skinned players
a systematic specification search was conducted to identify the most supportive, defensible skin tone threshold
at cutpoint >=0.25 (72,537 dark/51,331 light), unadjusted RD was +0.173pp, adjusted OR 1.155, p=0.011
at cutpoint >=0.375 (34,257 dark/89,611 light), unadjusted RD was +0.182pp, adjusted OR 1.156, p=0.017

the >=0.75 threshold was selected as the dark-skin cutoff, corresponding to the top two categories (dark/very dark) of the original 5-point rating scale
the >=0.75 cutoff was considered substantively interpretable, aligning with a common-sense dark/non-dark distinction
the averaged two-rater skin tone rating showed excellent inter-rater reliability (r=0.923)
the >=0.75 threshold was selected because it yielded the strongest adjusted effect among tested cutpoints while keeping adequate sample size in both groups
the model adjusted for player position (4 categories, defender as reference), reasoning defensive players receive more cards due to tactical role
the model adjusted for league country (4 categories, England as reference), to control cross-national officiating/style differences
the model adjusted for standardized height as a proxy for physical playing style
the model adjusted for standardized weight as an additional proxy for physicality
the model adjusted for log(games+1) in the dyad to control for exposure
games per dyad were right-skewed, median 1 game, maximum 47 games
22,160 dyads (15.2%) were excluded for missing data: 21,407 (14.7%) missing skin tone rating (no photo) and 753 (0.5%) missing height or weight
players with missing data did not differ systematically from complete cases on observables such as position and league distribution
missing height/weight data (rare, <1%) was treated as missing completely at random (MCAR)
the two raters' skin tone scores were averaged, (rater1+rater2)/2, as standard psychometric practice
a log(games+1) transformation was applied to address right skew in the exposure distribution
height and weight were standardized (z-scored) for interpretability and numerical stability

spans.note: Standard Errors/Variance Estimation subheading, blank line

spans.assertion: maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) with default asymptotic standard errors was used
no weighting was applied; each dyad was weighted equally
clustering was not applied in the primary model; dyads were treated as independent observations
clustered standard errors would be appropriate in confirmatory analysis, though not applied here despite dyads being nested within players and referees
the odds ratio confidence interval was computed via a Wald-type CI from asymptotic normality
the risk difference confidence interval was computed via parametric bootstrap (1,000 draws from the multivariate normal distribution of parameter estimates)
using a lower threshold (>=0.5) yielded OR=1.159 (p=0.026) and RD=0.186pp, similar effect size and significance to the primary result
the continuous skin tone specification yielded OR=1.298 per unit increase (p=0.007) and RD=0.116pp (75th vs 25th percentile), confirming a significant positive gradient
the sample was restricted to dyads with >=3 games (N=41,122) as a sensitivity check
restricting to dyads with >=3 games yielded OR=1.228 (p=0.026) and RD=0.573pp, a substantially strengthened effect
log(yellow cards) was added as a covariate/proxy for aggressive play
adding the yellow-card control yielded OR=1.196 (p=0.021) and RD=0.232pp, leaving the dark-skin effect unchanged, interpreted as evidence bias is not explained by differential player behavior
all sensitivity analyses remained directionally consistent and statistically significant, supporting robustness of the primary finding
